A legal memorandum examines the effect of Weisberg v. Department of Justice on another case, Center for National Policy Review v. Weinberger, in the D.C. Circuit, number 73-1090. Harold Weisberg's records suits made law that other litigants then had to reckon with. The memo works out what his precedent meant inside a live appeal.

Freedom of Information law was built case by case in this era, and Weisberg built more of it than most. A memo tracing his case's effect shows doctrine moving from one courtroom to another. The analysis preserves lawyers reading Weisberg the way later requesters would read them.
the-abbot-s-ghost-or-maurice-treherne-s-:
A. M. Barnard wrote The Abbot's Ghost, or Maurice Treherne's Temptation, as a Christmas story in 1867. Chapter one, headed Dramatis Personae, opens with talk before a fire in a grand house at the start of a holiday visit.

Frank and the Major trade barbs about lovely Octavia, the prize both men may seek, while fresh guests roll up by carriage. General Snowdon and his wife arrive, and Maurice Treherne has come while the men were out. The Major calls his case a hard one, and Frank presses for the facts before dinner. Readers get a country-house Christmas tale with a ghost, a crippled heir, and love crossed by pride and a dark house secret.
